Information Retrieval.title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
Information Retrieval.summary: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.
Information Retrieval.comment: Experiment one presented at the 48th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society as a full paper talk in "Collective Intelligence."

Machine Learning.title: The Statistical Benefits of Multiple Responses for Learning from Demonstrations
Machine Learning.summary: Many generative systems return multiple candidate responses and are evaluated according to the best one. Recent work shows that, when demonstrations are optimal, pass@$k$ can reduce the sample complexity of learning from demonstrations by a logarithmic factor in $k$. We ask what happens when the demonstrator is not assumed to be optimal. We find that multiple responses provide a qualitatively stronger benefit in this setting. In a finite reward-class model with no reward feedback, moving from pass@$1$ to any pass@$k$ with $k\ge2$ changes the worst-case dependence on target accuracy from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$, uniformly over demonstrator quality. Under standard evaluation, where an unknown reward is fixed before training, increasing $k$ provides an additional and distinct benefit: the optimal dependence on a reward class of size $N$ improves from $\log N$ to $\log N/\log k$. We further show that these two effects can be separated. Under robust evaluation, where one learned policy must compete with the demonstrator simultaneously for every reward in the class, the fast $1/\varepsilon$ dependence persists, while the $1/\log k$ improvement can disappear. We establish matching upper and lower bounds in the corresponding regimes and give a greedy multiplicative-weights learner achieving the upper bounds without any assumption on demonstrator quality.

Machine Learning.title: Steering Diffusion Models to Rare Events with Sequential Monte Carlo
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models are increasingly used as surrogates for expensive simulators in weather prediction, molecular dynamics, and materials design. In these models, computing the probability $p_0[E]$ of an event $E$ is difficult, especially when the event of interest is rare. A stable estimate using Monte Carlo becomes computationally intractable, requiring a growing sample size $\propto\!1/p_0[E]$ to compensate for an increasing rarity. In this paper, we present Diffusion rare event sampling with Sequential Monte Carlo (DireSMC), a sequential Monte Carlo scheme that guides a population of weighted samples towards the rare event, giving access not only to samples but also to a calibrated estimate of its probability. We set up our guidance using an analytical relaxation of the event set, allowing the method to easily extend to a wide range of user-defined rare events. We validate our method on a toy problem with analytical solutions and on a score-based climate emulator, where we obtain accurate rare-event probabilities on a range of rarities from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-5}$, achieving net speed-ups of $9\times$ to $1413\times$ over Monte Carlo.
Machine Learning.comment: A previous version of this work was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026: AI for Stochastic Dynamics workshop

Machine Learning.title: Multi-Sensitive Distributional Fairness: Joint Wasserstein Audits and Shapley Allocation
Machine Learning.summary: Fairness audits with several sensitive attributes are often performed one coordinate at a time. This can miss purely intersectional disparities: a score may be independent of each sensitive coordinate while depending on their joint profile. We study distributional demographic parity for a real-valued score using one-dimensional Wasserstein geometry. We distinguish two complementary constructions. Conditional and sequential audits characterize joint parity through their zero sets, but their positive values do not generally decompose a fixed joint Wasserstein disparity. By contrast, full-cell conditional quantile functions define a Hilbert-valued random variable whose variance is the joint disparity. Conditional expectations of this quantile process induce a monotone information game: every reveal order yields an exact martingale decomposition of the same joint disparity, while Shapley values provide an order-free attribution across sensitive attributes. Under independent sensitive attributes, the game reduces to a Hoeffding-ANOVA decomposition and Shapley splits each interaction energy equally among its members; under dependence, orthogonality is lost and explicit formulas reveal suppression and redundancy effects that marginal audits can hide. We give fixed-grid estimators and permutation calibration, and illustrate the framework on synthetic examples and ACSIncome. The resulting framework separates three questions that are often conflated: whether joint distributional parity holds, how a fixed joint disparity decomposes along an information path, and how that disparity can be attributed across sensitive coordinates without privileging an ordering.

Machine Learning.title: Generalizing Identifiability Results in Causal Discovery from Complete Data to Missing Data Settings
Machine Learning.summary: While causal discovery methods have matured for complete data, such algorithms for handling missing values remain limited. We establish general sufficient conditions under which causal graphs remain identifiable (i.e., uniquely determined from the available data distribution) under various missingness categories, including Missing Not At Random, and provide a framework to extend correctness guarantees from causal discovery algorithms for complete data to missing data settings. Our results show that identifiability of causal graphs with no unobserved confounders is preserved when (1) missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, (2) no variable directly causes its own missingness, and (3) either faithfulness holds for missingness mechanisms, or they follow generalized linear models. Guided by these theoretical results, we introduce two asymptotically correct algorithms for Additive Noise Models (ANMs) that recover the underlying causal graph and provide consistent parameter estimates.

Machine Learning.title: Embedding Geometry Shapes LLM Routing: Tracing Failure Modes and Improving Generalization
Machine Learning.summary: With the growing number of LLMs available, selecting which one to use for a prompt has become a key question. A large part of the routing literature relies on semantically embedding prompts into a vector space and then applying a lightweight classifier to the embedded representations. These methods perform robustly in-distribution but they struggle to generalize to unseen tasks. By studying the geometry of semantic embeddings, we trace a clear failure mode: features that determine the neighbors of unseen prompts are an unreliable proxy for LLM selection. We therefore replace the semantic embedding with the following map: we run a partial forward pass of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the prompt and use the hidden state of its last token at a deep layer as the representation. When applying kNN and other simple classifiers to this new representation, we obtain a clear result in generalization: on average across cost penalties, their performance improves. Moreover, kNN and another simple classifier that we propose outperform every evaluated semantic-embedding baseline. Our two simple methods also beat a recent SoTA hidden-states based router on RouterBench.

Machine Learning.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent
Machine Learning.summary: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.

Machine Learning.title: Robust inference for risk heterogeneity under group imbalance
Machine Learning.summary: Population-level heterogeneity is ubiquitous in biomedical data, where differences across demographic or clinical subgroups can substantially alter risk patterns. For example, in intensive care unit (ICU) studies, the mortality risk associated with specific admission diagnoses can vary across ethnic groups. Existing approaches for detecting risk heterogeneity are often sensitive to baseline model misspecification and regularization bias, both of which commonly arise in practice. In this paper, we propose a robust framework for inferring risk heterogeneity between two populations using Neyman orthogonality, which yields estimators that are locally insensitive to nuisance parameter estimation error. The proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and simulation studies demonstrate that in finite samples our method substantially reduces bias and improves inferential stability compared with standard likelihood-based approaches. In an application to the eICU Collaborative Research Database, our method reveals clinically meaningful ethnicity-specific heterogeneity in admission diagnoses for in-hospital mortality that standard likelihood-based methods fail to detect.

Machine Learning.title: When Can Digital Personas Reliably Approximate Human Survey Findings?
Machine Learning.summary: Digital personas powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human survey respondents, yet it remains unclear when they can reliably approximate human survey findings. We answer this question using the LISS panel, constructing personas from respondents' background variables and pre-2023 survey histories, then testing them against the same respondents' held-out post-cutoff answers. Across four persona architectures, three LLMs, and two prediction tasks, we assess performance at the question, respondent, distributional, equity, and clustering levels. Digital personas improve alignment with human response distributions, especially in domains tied to stable attributes and values, but remain limited for individual prediction and fail to recover multivariate respondent structure. Retrieval-augmented architectures provide the clearest gains, but performance depends more on human response structure than on model choice: personas perform best for low-variability questions and common respondent patterns, and worst for subjective, heterogeneous, or rare responses. Our results provide practical guidance on when digital personas could be appropriate for survey research and when human validation remains necessary.

Machine Learning.title: Student Copula Markov Networks
Machine Learning.summary: This paper extends the applicability of probabilistic graphical models to non Gaussian data. It establishes a characterization of the pairwise Markov property in undirected probabilistic graphical models in terms of copula densities. Building on this characterization, we derive a necessary condition for the pairwise Markov property in Student copula Markov networks. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm (ECM) is provided to facilitate the penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies, which demonstrate its effectiveness in estimating model parameters and recovering the underlying graph structure.

Machine Learning.title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments
Machine Learning.summary: Learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR) with many treatments requires estimating treatment-specific effects from limited observations per arm. Treatments with similar conditional responses can share information, but linear contrast models may miss nonlinear heterogeneity. We propose nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (NSCF), a neural Q-learning framework with a shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings. Pairwise fusion groups treatments with similar learned contrasts, yielding an ITR and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, validation-based partition selection, and unpenalized grouped refitting. NSCF lowers regret relative to a strong neural reference in nonlinear exact-sharing simulations; perturbations characterize the limits of hard sharing. In a melanoma xenograft application, NSCF improves average policy value over the neural reference. These results support nonlinear representation learning with supervised treatment fusion when treatment effects exhibit shared structure.

Machine Learning.title: Sig-DEG for Distillation: Making Diffusion Models Faster and Lighter
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art generative performance but remain computationally expensive at inference, often requiring many discretization steps. We propose Sig-DEG (Signature-based Differential Equation Generator), a generator for distilling pre-trained diffusion models. Inspired by high-order stochastic Taylor expansions, Sig-DEG combines partial signatures that summarize Brownian motion over subintervals with a recurrent structure to approximate stochastic differential equation solutions to achieve universality. We formulate distillation as supervised learning, matching fine-resolution teacher trajectories on a coarse time grid. At inference, Sig-DEG enables fast generation, as the partial signatures can be simulated exactly from their known distributions without requiring fine-grained Brownian paths. Experiments on image and time-series generation demonstrate competitive sample quality with inference speedups of up to several hundred times over the teacher. A Schrödinger bridge example further demonstrates Sig-DEG's applicability beyond diffusion distillation.
Machine Learning.comment: 44 pages. Revised version with expanded theoretical analysis, updated experiments, and revised presentation

Machine Learning.title: ProximalFM: Amortized Proximal Causal Inference under Hidden Confounding
Machine Learning.summary: Standard causal identification methods often assume no unmeasured confounding and can fail when relevant confounders are unobserved. Proximal causal inference instead uses proxy variables to identify effects under hidden confounding. However, nonparametric proximal estimation can be challenging in practice: recovering causal estimands such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) requires solving an ill-posed integral equation that is data-hungry, hyperparameter-sensitive, and optimization-unstable. Bayesian inference for such models provides a desirable alternative, mitigating these difficulties by regularizing through the prior. However, computing a posterior is itself challenging, as a typical likelihood function will include latent variables. Following the recent success of tabular foundation models in backdoor, instrumental variable, and frontdoor settings, we propose that prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are uniquely suited to resolve this bottleneck. Indeed, by training on synthetic data sampled from compliant structural causal models with access to oracle counterfactuals, we simplify the task substantially, amortizing the implied Bayesian operator inversion into a single transformer forward pass. Compared to prior literature that focuses primarily on point estimation, our model, ProximalFM, explicitly targets the Bayesian posterior distribution of the CATE. One unique aspect of this problem is that we need to provide Monte Carlo estimates of the oracle CATEs, leading to a novel variation of PFNs that accounts for the added stochastic error. Across a diverse suite of proximal regimes, ProximalFM achieves consistently strong CATE-estimation performance without dataset-specific tuning, with its largest advantage when latent confounding is substantial and the proxies are weakly informative; it also provides fast inference through a single amortized forward pass.

Machine Learning.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models
Machine Learning.summary: Compartment models of infectious diseases are often linear in coefficients that are physical parameters or products or ratios of them. We exploit this with closed-form least squares and equip the estimates with distribution-free uncertainty. Physics-informed regression (PIR) fits the parameters to finite-difference derivatives of the data; we introduce physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), which integrates the model in time instead, needs no derivatives of the data, estimates the initial state jointly and is high-order accurate. To quantify uncertainty we wrap both estimators in split conformal prediction, with a calibration population generated by the physics-based model itself, giving simultaneous intervals for all parameters with a finite-sample coverage guarantee. A residual-adaptive factor, computed without ground truth, scales the intervals to each data set (PIWR-RACC). On the eleven benchmark models of disease-informed neural networks (DINNs), PIWR or PIR-FD6 is one to four orders of magnitude more accurate than the reported DINN results wherever the sampling resolves the dynamics, in about a millisecond per fit instead of minutes to hours of training, and the 90% intervals achieve 87-92% coverage in all 88 settings. On the S3I3R model of the original PIR study, PIWR lowers the reported PIR errors by about three orders of magnitude. On real data from the 1978 boarding-school influenza outbreak, a variable-projection variant gives calibrated 95% intervals that overlap those of a Bayesian analysis. On a time-varying transmission benchmark, a B-spline expansion of beta(t) keeps PIR and PIWR linear; they are more accurate than physics-informed neural networks in three of four cases and comparable in the noisiest, with simultaneous bands for beta(t). The complete conformal calibration takes less than two minutes for every benchmark.
Machine Learning.comment: 30 pages (incl. appendix), 7 figures in total 20 tables (9 in main text and 11 in appendix)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Job Assignment
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Motivated primarily by applications in cloud computing, we study a simple, yet powerful, online allocation problem in which jobs of varying durations arrive over continuous time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably to one of the available offline servers. Each server has a fixed initial capacity, with assigned jobs occupying one unit for their duration and releasing it upon completion. The algorithm earns a reward for each assignment upon completion. We consider a general heterogeneous setting where both the reward and duration of a job depend on the job-server pair. The objective of the online algorithm is to maximize the total collected reward, and remain competitive against an omniscient benchmark that knows all job arrivals in advance. Our main contribution is the design of a new online algorithm, termed Forward-Looking BALANCE (FLB), and using primal-dual framework to establish that it is (asymptotically) optimal-competitive.
  This meta-algorithm has two main primitives: (i) keeping track of the capacity used for each server at each time and applying a penalty function to this quantity, and (ii) adjusting the reward of assigning a job to a server by subtracting the total penalty of a particularly chosen subset of future times, in contrast to just looking at the current time. The FLB algorithm then assigns the arriving job to the server with the maximum adjusted reward. If R and D are the ratios of maximum over minimum rewards and durations, we show that the FLB algorithm obtains an asymptotic competitive ratio of ln(RD)+3lnln(max(R,D))+O(1). We further show this bound has optimal dependencies on all the parameters. Our main analysis combines a novel dual-fitting technique, which leverages the configuration LP benchmark for this problem, and a novel inductive argument to establish the capacity feasibility of the algorithm, which might be of independent interest.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Unit-Demand Pricing for Min-Buying Customers
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the unit-demand pricing problem under \textit{min-buying} behavior, where customers purchase the lowest-priced item that yields non-negative utility. In contrast to the quasi-linear model, we show that uniform pricing becomes substantially more effective under min-buying. First, we study symmetric environments. We show that for min-buying customers with independent and identically distributed valuations, a uniform price across items is optimal. We then extend this optimality result to all valuations drawn from exchangeable and affiliated distributions. However, uniform pricing is not optimal in all symmetric environments: for min-buying customers we construct an exchangeable and non-affiliated valuation distribution for which the gap between uniform pricing and optimal item pricing is logarithmic in the number of items. This gap is tight and matches the worst-case gap in the quasi-linear setting. Next, we consider asymmetric environments in which valuations are independent but not identically distributed. When these valuations are regular and customers are min-buying, we show that a uniform price guarantees approximately 69.86\% of the optimal item-pricing revenue and this is tight. Overall, our results highlight that the value of non-uniform pricing substantially diminishes, and often disappears entirely, under more conservative demand models in which customers engage in satisficing behaviors such as min-buying.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Stochastic Growth Model for Online Platforms
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We investigate the growth trajectory of online platforms operating as market makers in two-sided matching markets. Their expansion, often referred to as the ``chicken-and-egg dilemma'' in the literature, poses an inherent challenge: service providers find value in joining the platform because of the presence of customers, while customers are drawn to the platform by the availability of service providers. Much of the existing literature addresses this expansion challenge through either a static market-clearing lens or aggregate dynamic models, emphasizing how network externalities shape a platform's growth trajectory and equilibrium size. These approaches do not fully capture how gradual growth must be implemented through server-level admission, assignment, and compensation decisions. Embedded in this growth process are intertemporal participation constraints that the platform must satisfy to attract and retain forward-looking servers.
  To explicitly account for the stochastic dynamics of a platform's gradual growth, we model the system as a Markov process. Potential servers and customers arrive according to Poisson processes, and customer demand is non-decreasing in the number of active servers. Under mild conditions, we characterize the platform's optimal admission, assignment, and compensation policies. The platform admits servers at the maximum feasible rate until it reaches an endogenous target size, which can be smaller than the static market-clearing optimum. In the baseline model, seniority-based compensation acts as an operational substitute for financially subsidized growth: instead of using upfront subsidies to induce early server participation, the platform uses future cash flows to reward early servers for joining when demand is limited and for helping the platform reach later, higher-demand states.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Resource Allocation with Cancellations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We initiate the study of two-sided online resource allocation with costly cancellations within the buyback model. Our focus is on edge-weighted online matching and several of its extensions. In our base matching model, nodes arrive online on one side and request offline resources on the other side. In contrast to the classic literature, in our model the decision maker can reclaim any fraction of an offline resource that was preallocated to an earlier online node. However, reclaiming a resource not only results in the loss of the previously allocated edge-weight but also incurs an additional penalty equal to a non-negative constant factor $f$ times the edge-weight. Parameterizing the problem by the buyback factor $f$, our main result is the development of optimal competitive algorithms for \emph{all possible values} of $f$ through a novel primal-dual family of algorithms in the fractional (or equivalently, large capacity) setting. We establish the optimality of our results by deriving separate lower bounds for both the small and large buyback factor regimes and showing that our primal-dual algorithm exactly matches these lower bounds by appropriately tuning a parameter as a function of $f$. Interestingly, our results reveal a phase transition: for the small buyback regime ($f < \frac{e-2}{2}$), the optimal competitive ratio is $\frac{e}{e-(1+f)}$, and for the large buyback regime ($f \geq \frac{e-2}{2}$), the competitive ratio is $-W_{-1}\left(\frac{-1}{e(1+f)}\right)$, where $W_{-1}$ is the non-principal branch of the Lambert $W$ function.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: A preliminary conference version of this work has appeared in the ACM Economics and Computations(EC) 2023 conference under the title "Online Resource Allocation with Buyback: Optimal Algorithms via Primal-Dual." ; An earlier version of this paper was distributed under the title "Online Matching with Cancellation Costs."

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand.
  Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness.
  Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Tractability Boundary for Exclusion Zones in Instant-Runoff Voting: Planar Versus One-Apex Graphs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study exclusion zones for instant-runoff voting (IRV) on connected, unweighted graphs. Each vertex hosts one voter and may host a candidate. Voters rank candidates by shortest-path distance and cast one whole vote in each round. Distance ties favour the smaller identifier in a common fixed vertex ordering, and equal-score elimination ties remove the larger identifier in that ordering. A nonempty vertex set $S$ is an exclusion zone if every election with at least one participating candidate in $S$ elects a winner in $S$. In this setting, we consider three computational problems: deciding whether a target candidate can lose against some nonempty subset of a given set of allowed opponents, deciding whether a given vertex subset is an exclusion zone, and computing the unique minimum exclusion zone. We establish that all three are polynomial-time solvable on trees, outerplanar graphs and, more generally, planar graphs. For an n-vertex tree, the first problem (candidate loss) can be decided in O(n) time. The planar algorithm uses the structure of an inclusion-minimal candidate set that eliminates the target in the first round: contracting the candidates' voter cells makes the target cell adjacent to every other cell, leading to bounded-width structure and enumerable separators. We give explicit implementations and conservative polynomial running-time and space bounds; the large exponents for outerplanar and planar graphs establish tractability rather than practical efficiency. In contrast, even on bipartite exact one-apex graphs of bounded diameter with every nontarget vertex eligible to stand, candidate loss is NP-complete, singleton-zone verification is coNP-complete, and the minimum exclusion zone cannot be computed in polynomial time unless P = coNP. Thus planarity marks a tractability boundary for these computational problems under the voting and tie-breaking conventions studied here.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 66 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: An Introduction to Contract Theory for Computer Scientists
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This survey introduces contract design to computer scientists: using outcome-based payments to incentivize effort. We discuss applications that motivate a computational approach to contract design, ranging from online labor markets, to incentive-aware algorithmic classification, to emerging ecosystems of AI agents. We present the classic principal-agent model and introduce basic concepts. We show how optimal contracts are computable via linear programming, and why they can be opaque and brittle. Motivated by this we turn to simpler contract formats, specifically linear contracts. We discuss approximation guarantees, and robust (max-min) optimality of such contracts. We then move beyond the single-agent setting to combinatorial contract settings with multiple agents, mapping the algorithmic landscape of tractability and approximation. Finally, we discuss partial information settings through the lens of learning algorithms, and outline open directions. The goal is a concise, accessible entry point that connects economic foundations with algorithmic tools and highlights opportunities for new theory and applications.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Large player classes and approximately weighted voting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: It is known that completeness of the coalitional ($C$-)desirability relation in a simple game does not imply the existence of a weighted-majority representation. We show that weightedness is implied in an approximate sense. Call an $n$-player simple game $\varepsilon$-weighted if, for some weight vector in the $(n-1)$-simplex, any losing coalition weight exceeds any winning coalition weight by at most $\varepsilon$; let $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ be the smallest such $\varepsilon$. We establish an upper bound on $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ in a general $C$-complete game, and deduce that, if all classes of equally desirable players become large asymptotically but the number of classes is bounded, then $\varepsilon^{\ast}=O(1/n_{\min})$ for the minimal player class size $n_{\min}$, and the bound is tight. Importantly, the minimal attainable fraction $δ$ of coalitions mislabeled by a weighting rule also tends to $0$ when $n_{\min}\rightarrow\infty$ and the number of player classes is bounded, with $δ=O(1/\sqrt{n_{\min}})$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft II: Simulations and Marketplace Analysis
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Ride-hailing platforms increasingly face uncertain driver acceptance, which makes traditional one-to-one \emph{exclusive dispatch} (ED) less efficient: rejections and timeouts force sequential retries and lengthen rider wait times, which in turn creates friction in the marketplace. \emph{Non-exclusive dispatch} (NED) mitigates this friction by broadcasting a request to multiple drivers in parallel. While NED can reduce latency, it introduces new design challenges---most notably, how to choose notification sets and how to resolve driver contention (when multiple drivers accept the same ride).
  In this paper---the second in a two-part collaboration with Lyft---we develop a theoretically grounded framework to evaluate the long-run performance and marketplace effects of transitioning from ED to NED. We bridge theory and practice by combining (i) an optimization model that formulates NED as a constrained welfare maximization problem with (ii) large-scale discrete-event simulations on proprietary Lyft traces and (iii) a stylized macroscopic equilibrium model. Across simulation and equilibrium analysis, we find that NED improves key fulfillment metrics relative to ED: it reduces match time (and hence rider reneging) while increasing both the number and the average quality of completed matches. We also quantify the speed--quality trade-off between two common contention resolution rules, \emph{First-Accept} and \emph{Best-Accept}: First-Accept maximizes speed and throughput, whereas Best-Accept is required to maximize per-match quality. Finally, we show that slightly conservative notification heuristics can improve long-run efficiency by avoiding excessive locking of high-value drivers and preserving future availability.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft I: Single-Cycle Approximation Algorithms
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Ride-hailing platforms increasingly rely on non-exclusive notifications--broadcasting a single request to multiple drivers simultaneously--to mitigate inefficiencies caused by uncertain driver acceptance. In this paper, the first in a two-part collaboration with Lyft, we formally model the Notification Set Selection Problem for a single decision cycle, where the platform determines the optimal subset of drivers to notify for each incoming ride request. We analyze this combinatorial optimization problem under two contention-resolution protocols: First Acceptance (FA), which prioritizes speed by assigning the ride to the first responder, and Best Acceptance (BA), which prioritizes match quality by selecting the highest-valued accepting driver.
  We show that welfare maximization under both mechanisms is NP-hard, ruling out a polynomial-time exact algorithm unless P=NP. Despite this hardness, we establish several positive algorithmic results. For FA, we develop a Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) for the single-rider problem. For the general matching setting, we provide a (1-1/e)-approximation algorithm that applies to both FA and BA. Along the way, we show that the FA valuation function constitutes a novel discrete choice model with structural properties of independent interest. For BA, we further prove that the welfare objective is monotone and submodular and exploit additional structure to obtain an approximation guarantee that surpasses the classical (1-1/e) barrier. Finally, when acceptance probabilities are independent of the drivers, we show that the BA problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time through a linear programming formulation. We evaluate our algorithms on synthetic instances and on instances calibrated using real ride-sharing data from Lyft, demonstrating strong empirical performance.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Fair Division with Upgrade Recourse
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the online fair division of indivisible goods. In the standard model, where assignments are irrevocable, no algorithm can guarantee any positive fraction of the maximin share (MMS). Reassigning earlier goods can restore fairness, but it may take value away from agents who already hold them. We ask how much fairness can be maintained if every reassignment must leave each affected agent at least as well off. We consider two forms of such upgrade recourse. Under item-level upgrades, each good an agent holds must be kept or replaced by a distinct good she values at least as much; under bundle-level upgrades, only her total value must not decrease. For item-level upgrades, we show that the optimal MMS factor is essentially $1/H_n \approx 1/\ln n$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number, and that fixed picking sequences nearly attain it. Since these sequences use only the agents' rankings of individual goods, knowing the actual values cannot improve the optimal factor for up to 33 agents, and improves it by at most a vanishing margin as $n$ grows. Bundle-level upgrades allow substantially stronger guarantees. By permitting several-for-one exchanges, they turn this vanishing factor into a constant: we achieve exact MMS for two agents and more than half of MMS for any number of agents, in both cases together with relaxations of envy-freeness. Finally, we show that predictions about future goods let online algorithms inherit any offline MMS guarantee, losing only an additive term bounded by the prediction error. Under item-level upgrades, however, insisting on exact MMS when predictions are correct leaves no positive guarantee when they are wrong.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Prophet Inequalities with Cancellation Costs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Most of the literature on online algorithms and sequential decision-making in revenue management focuses on settings with irrevocable decisions. Motivated by modern applications such as cloud spot markets, selling banner ads, and online hotel booking, we study "prophet inequalities with cancellations" under linear cancellation costs (the buyback model). A sequence of independent random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ with known distributions is revealed one by one. After accepting $X_j$, a decision-maker may later discard it and accept another variable at a cost of $f \times X_j$, where $f \ge 0$. The goal is to maximize the expected net reward: the value of the final accepted variable minus the total cancellation cost. We compare online policies with an omniscient optimal offline "prophet" benchmark.
  Our first main result is an optimal prophet inequality for all parameters $f \ge 0$. We fully characterize the worst-case competitive ratio of the optimal online policy against the optimal offline benchmark via a differential equation, for which we provide a constructive solution. Our second main result is a simple polynomial-time randomized adaptive policy that achieves this optimal competitive ratio. Our policy is order-agnostic (in the sense of Samuel-Cahn (1984)): it only needs to know the set of distributions and not their arrival order. These results follow from reductions to a continuous "generalized flow problem," viewed as the dual to a factor-revealing LP for the worst-case competitive ratio. Our techniques include a geometric interpretation of its solution via a differential equation and the embedding of random variables into specific Poisson point processes. We also use these building blocks to construct lower-bound instances and to design and analyze our
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: The first conference version of this paper has appeared in the ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 2024), and the second conference version has appeared in the ACM Economics and Computations (EC 2026)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Complexity of Exact and Approximate Nash Equilibria in Anonymous Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We prove that, for every fixed rational $c>0$, computing a $2^{-n^c}$-approximate Nash equilibrium in an $n$-player two-strategy anonymous game is $\mathsf{PPAD}$-complete. This holds even when one strategy always pays $1/2$ and, for all but two players, the other is constant outside at most five opponent counts. The reduction uses coefficient estimates to simulate circuit constraints approximately. Exact computation requires eliminating the simulation error: with three strategies, a separate construction uses polynomial roots to implement circuit gates exactly. This yields $\mathsf{FIXP}$-completeness of exact equilibrium computation under separable-linear reductions and $\mathsf{FIXP}_a$-completeness of approximation in distance to an exact equilibrium.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 48 pages, including appendices and references; 2 figures and 4 tables

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A $1/2$-Approximation for Pandora's Problem with Deadlines
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Pandora's problem is a fundamental model of sequential search in which opening each box incurs a cost. We study the variant with deadlines, where each box has a publicly known deadline for both opening and selection. We prove that a simple threshold strategy achieves a $1/2$-approximation to the optimal expected utility, improving the previous guarantee arbitrarily close to $1/4$ due to Amanatidis et al. (2025).

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Digital Twin (DT) combined with reinforcement learning (RL) can support adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making by comparing expected and observed network behavior. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network. For each action, the same channel simulator is evaluated under an attack-free and an attacked configuration. Receiver-level residuals are combined with spatial jamming footprints and accumulated to form a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into an aggregated state, a belief-concentration reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. The BGQL scheme is compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random under matched attacker sets. Across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs in four configurations, with the number of active jammers supplied to every method, BGQL achieves mean aggregate full-band link-rate scores of approximately 437.4--564.2~Mbit/s and rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37--76.79~Mbit/J. Its detection accuracy is 100\% in one-jammer configurations and approximately 78\%--81\% in two-jammer configurations. BGQL requires approximately 80--130~s per run, compared with 5--14~s for SARSA, reflecting evaluation of 625 beam pairs during exploratory steps. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Voter Model with Opinion Graph
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the \emph{voter model with opinion graph}, a generalization of the standard (pull) voter model that adds a notion of bounded confidence. In this process, we consider a finite set $A$ of $n$ agents. Each agent $u \in A$ has an opinion $x_u \in O$, where we model opinions as vertices in an undirected opinion graph $G = (O,E)$ with $|O|=q$. In each step, an agent $u$ interacts with another agent $v \in A$. In contrast to classical voting, $u$ adopts the opinion $x_v$ if and only if $x_v$ and $x_u$ are neighbors in $G$. The process is stable once all remaining opinions are an independent set in $G$. We analyze two variants of the process: the ordinary EdgeVOG process, which samples a pair of interacting agents uniformly at random from all possible pairs, and the productive EdgeVOG process, which samples only pairs with neighboring opinions in $G$.
  We show the following:
  - For every opinion graph and every initial configuration, ordinary EdgeVOG stabilizes within $O(n^2\log n)$ steps in expectation and with high probability. The expectation bound is asymptotically tight. For the productive EdgeVOG process, the expected stabilization time is exactly the initial number of compatible agent pairs, while $O(n^2\log n)$ steps suffice with high probability.
  - An opinion $i$ with initial support $s_i$ survives with probability at least $p_i:=s_i/(s_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}s_j)$. Further, let $μ= \sum_{i \in O} p_i$, then we show the probability that less than $(1-δ)μ$ opinions survive is at most $\exp(-δ^2μ/(2(Δ^2+1)))$ for every $0\leqδ\leq1$.
  -If $G$ has maximum degree $Δ$ and every opinion initially has support at most $\hat{s}$, then no opinion ever acquires more than $\tilde{O}(\min\{n,Δ^6\hat{s}\})$ agents with high probability. This yields near-linear stabilization bounds for productive EdgeVOG for a large class of configurations.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Abstract shortened to comply Arxiv requirements

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: (Un)Decidability of Two-Clock Weighted Timed Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The Value Problem for weighted timed games consists in determining, given a two-player weighted timed game with a reachability objective and a rational threshold, whether or not the value of the game exceeds the threshold. This problem is known to be undecidable for weighted timed games with three or more clocks, and decidable for one-clock weighted timed games.
  In this paper, we settle the remaining two-clock case, which has remained stubbornly open for a decade. We show that two-clock weighted timed games lie precisely at the decidability frontier: On the one hand the Value problem is undecidable for two-clock weighted timed games, even when restricted to non-negative weights and under a time bound; On the other hand, we establish decidability under an almost divergence restriction, by providing a $3$\textsc{ExpTime} algorithm for computing the value of almost divergent turn-based two-clock weighted timed games.

Information Retrieval.title: FidLIF: Parallel Training of High-Fidelity Spiking Neurons with Exact BPTT
Information Retrieval.summary: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) show promise in energy-efficient computing through event-driven computation and stateful temporal processing, their recurrent membrane dynamics render their training inherently sequential and inefficient for long sequences. Existing methods achieve full-sequence parallelism in SNNs through two main strategies: redesigning or approximating spiking dynamics to avoid reset-coupled temporal dependencies, or relying on iterative relaxed fixed-point solvers that suffer from excessive memory costs and iteration-dependent backward overhead. To address these limitations, we present FidLIF, a novel framework that reconciles the incremental update and hard-reset behavior of standard spiking LIF neurons with parallel forward propagation and BPTT-equivalent backward propagation. FidLIF iteratively recovers the full-sequence membrane-potential trajectory in parallel. By exploiting the lower bidiagonal structure induced by the local recurrence of LIF neurons, FidLIF formulates each forward trajectory correction and backward adjoint propagation as associative scans with an $O(\log T)$ temporal depth. This formulation also supports input-dependent neuronal parameters and allows the same neuron to perform full-sequence parallel training and incremental step-by-step inference at deployment. In our numerical convergence evaluation, FidLIF achieves a mean absolute error below $10^{-7}$ relative to the matched serial relaxed LIF dynamics, while yielding gradients numerically equivalent to exact BPTT. Our Triton implementation delivers favorable long-sequence latency and memory scaling, while achieving competitive performance on four sequential classification benchmarks. By reconciling parallel training with step-by-step execution, FidLIF enables high-fidelity spiking dynamics to benefit from parallel hardware without compromising incremental inference at deployment.

Information Retrieval.title: Time Window Optimization for Motor Imagery Classification via Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning
Information Retrieval.summary: Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) typically decode continuous EEG using fixed-length sliding windows that may be misaligned with neural events. Existing window optimization methods often evaluate windows independently, overlooking temporal dependencies and potentially producing fragmented or physiologically implausible selections. We propose Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning (TSE-RL), a framework that incorporates prior knowledge of MI event structure into a constrained Markov decision process for adaptive window optimization. First, TSE-RL assigns each window an explicit semantic role through Discard, Onset, Sustain, or Offset actions, extending binary retain/discard decisions to event-level alignment. Second, a finite-state machine masks invalid actions to enforce the temporal order of MI phases and promote physiologically plausible window sequences. Third, a Transformer-based history encoder captures dependencies across windows, improving training stability and computational efficiency compared with recurrent architectures. TSE-RL is plug-and-play and can be integrated with diverse MI classifiers. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in decoding performance in both cross-session and cross-subject settings. Visualization analyses further suggest that the learned window selection policy aligns with neurophysiological principles.
Information Retrieval.comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Code available at https://github.com/LunaLab-XJTU/TSE-RL

Information Retrieval.title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
Information Retrieval.summary: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. The key difficulty is that neural architectures are operation-labeled DAGs: edge direction defines computational flow, but existing predictors often treat direction as a local structural cue. We propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer based on encoder-wide directional consistency, which preserves directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature update. DTA-GT realizes this principle with direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spectral controls show that the improvements come from coordinated direction-aware stages and edge-orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics confirm that the modules exhibit the intended directional behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 36 pages, 6 figures

Information Retrieval.title: TurboEvolve: Towards Fast and Robust LLM-Driven Program Evolution
Information Retrieval.summary: LLM-driven program evolution can discover high-quality programs, but high API cost and run-to-run variance hinder reliable progress. We propose TurboEvolve, a multi-island evolutionary framework that improves sample efficiency and stability under matched API-cost budgets. Inspired by multiple-offspring strategies in evolutionary algorithms, TurboEvolve introduces Verbalized Sampling, which elicits K diverse candidates in one LLM call while using self-assigned probabilities only as generation signals, together with an online scheduler that adapts K to expand exploration under stagnation and reduce redundant generation during steady progress. To exploit existing solution pools, TurboEvolve further introduces island-aware initialization, which clusters seed programs into mode-specific subpopulations and applies controlled cross-cluster mixing with elitist preservation to balance diversity, sharing, and refinement. We also curate a reusable cross-task solution-pool dataset to support warm-start initialization studies and matched-resource comparisons. Across mathematical discovery and GPU-kernel optimization tasks, TurboEvolve achieves stronger cost-quality trade-offs and more stable performance than controlled baselines, while reaching competitive reported scores.
Information Retrieval.comment: 12 pages, 8 figures

Information Retrieval.title: naspaclust: A hybridisation of spatial fuzzy clustering with nature-inspired optimisation
Information Retrieval.summary: We present an overview of R package called \texttt{naspaclust}, a tool for spatial fuzzy clustering improvement by hybridising the Fuzzy Geographically Weighted Clustering (FGWC) with nature-inspired optimisation algorithms. There are seven optimisation algorithms in general, namely Artificial Bee Colony, Flower Pollination Algorithm, Gravitational Search Algorithm, Harris-Hawk Optimisation, Intelligent Firefly Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimisation, and Teaching-Learning Based optimisation. The optimisation algorithms available do not only use the basic algorithms, but also the modified version of several parts such as randomisation terms and updating rules. Furthermore, we also provide additional options by providing more distance metrics options based on the \texttt{ rdist} package. This study showed the implementation of the \texttt{naspaclust} package in various cases, as well as comparing the performance of the algorithms in the scope of basic algorithms. The \texttt{naspaclust} package allows to improve the performance of fuzzy clustering, mainly in spatial context.
Information Retrieval.comment: 42 pages, 4 figures

Information Retrieval.title: How Biological Synapses Self-Assemble Gradient Learning
Information Retrieval.summary: Existing models of learning in the brain explain how given circuits learn, but not how biology could assemble those circuits in the first place. To address this gap, we formulate Self-Assembling Learning (SAL)---the study of how learning systems can emerge from lower-level interactions---and introduce one example mechanism, the Self-Assembling Motif (SAM). SAM is self-assembling at two scales: the motif emerges from initially random connectivity under heterosynaptic plasticity rules, and networks of SAMs, composed hierarchically, self-organize into dynamics that provably approximate a generalized form of stochastic gradient descent---matching backpropagation-level performance. This suggests that biological learning need not be prescribed but can emerge from local rules---and to a far greater extent than previously thought.
Information Retrieval.comment: Authors' manuscript, including supporting information

Information Retrieval.title: CIPHEUR: LLM-Guided Structural Search Control for Conflict-Graph Optimization
Information Retrieval.summary: Conflict-graph search can stagnate despite effective operators when interventions fail to address the conflicts blocking progress. A disruptive intervention may also require further search before its value emerges. We propose CIPHEUR, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that connects conflict evidence to coordinated intervention and recovery through Structured Intervention Units (SIUs). The shared control interface supports offline synthesis of executable policies and online contextual decisions. Asynchronous online control sustains native search during inference, while all policies preserve the original objective and feasibility constraints. Across eight satellite-ground scheduling conflict views with five runs per view and a 900-second evaluation cap, CIPHEUR-online achieves the highest mean objective among 11 configurations and increases mean scheduled contact duration by 14.84% over the greedy baseline GWMIN. It exceeds the strongest external per-view mean in seven of eight views and outperforms CHILS in all 40 paired runs. Within the same runs, its normalized objective improvement from 360 to 900 seconds is 1.50 to 1.86 times that of the two programmatic controllers. A separately frozen, one-shot LLM-generated controller also improves the mean objective over CHILS without runtime model calls. Together, these results demonstrate how structural search control translates LLM design knowledge and contextual reasoning into improved solution quality and sustained search progress.

Information Retrieval.title: AutoPSO: A Meta-framework for Automated Particle Swarm Optimization
Information Retrieval.summary: Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a widely used metaheuristic, prized for its simplicity and small parameter set. Although decades of research have produced numerous PSO variants that improve performance by modifying key components (e.g., parameter schedules, swarm topologies, or updating rules), two fundamental challenges persist. First, most existing approaches are problem-specific and hand-crafted, leading to poor cross-task generalization and forcing practitioners to navigate an impractically large design space, which also hinders systematic reuse of prior effective mechanisms. Second, mainstream implementations remain CPU-bound, constraining scalability and substantially increasing computational cost in real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose AutoPSO, a highly automated meta-framework for constructing customized PSO algorithms. AutoPSO formulates PSO-based optimization as a bi-level process: an outer search explores the joint space of effective PSO components, while an inner loop instantiates candidate variants to solve the target task and provide feedback. The outer search operates over a curated, open-design component pool, supporting flexible replacement of the component set and the outer optimizer. Crucially, by leveraging EvoX for population tensorization and batched evaluations, AutoPSO can efficiently assess thousands of particles within practical time budgets. Comprehensive experiments on numerical benchmarks and neuroevolution robotic control tasks demonstrate that AutoPSO consistently discovers novel PSO variants that significantly outperform strong baselines. Ablation and scalability studies further highlight the contribution of individual algorithmic components and confirm that AutoPSO achieves increasing performance gains with larger swarm sizes. Code is available at {https://github.com/EMI-Group/autopso}.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted by IEEE TEVC

Information Retrieval.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
Information Retrieval.summary: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of one memory substrate than as a kind of content. The substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM (commercial SRAM-CAM) and PyVaCoAl (DRAM-CAM).In VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl a directed acyclic graph (DAG) reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue mode) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating collisions (Don't Care mode) yields a path-integrated confidence, CR$_2$, that silently favours direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity is a formal counterpart of Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only in a regime where it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding, the Identikit as role-filler composition, recognition as majority-vote coincidence. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as attending to his fingers can make Polanyi's pianist falter, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this but narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell contingent from regime-bound tacitness. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. (5) Terence Tao's remark that AI-solved problems spawn few follow-ups is diagnosed as rootless explicit knowledge: checkable results whose route no one can follow and that no one yet understands well enough to extend, teach or judge. To re-root them, LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps an auditable trace with its confidence, and people value, a role virtue epistemology shows cannot be offloaded. Testable predictions follow.
Information Retrieval.comment: 27 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures

Information Retrieval.title: NeuroRule: Making Black-Box Neural Networks Explainable through Rule-set Evolution
Information Retrieval.summary: High-capacity neural network models have achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse classification tasks, yet they frequently operate as black-box models, lacking the transparency necessary for critical decision-making. Such opacity creates a persistent trade-off between performance and explainability. This paper proposes a solution to address this gap: the NeuroRule knowledge distillation framework that results in explainable rule-sets from neural network models. NeuroRule adapts the EVOTER rule-set evolution infrastructure to treat neural networks as targets for the evolution process, distilling their performance into concise sets of propositional logic expressions. There are three primary contributions: (1) an evolutionary method for distilling black-box neural network models into explicit rule-set models; (2) a method for making rule sets more explainable by including a conciseness objective to evolution; and (3) a demonstration that the distillation is viable even without access to the original neural network training data. The paper thus establishes that black-box neural network models can be made explainable and therefore useful in real-world applications where trustworthiness is paramount.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 41 pages, 11 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $Ω((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 37 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Inverting Top Trading Cycles: Characterizing the Endowments that Implement a Pareto-Optimal Allocation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In one-sided matching with strict ordinal preferences, the Top Trading Cycles (TTC) mechanism maps every initial endowment to a Pareto-optimal (PO) allocation, and many distinct endowments converge to the same outcome. We study the \emph{inverse} problem: given a PO allocation $σ$, characterize and enumerate its preimage $f^{-1}(σ)$, the set of endowments from which TTC produces $σ$. We characterize $f^{-1}(σ)$ via ordered partitions of the agents and present a sound and complete enumeration algorithm, invTTC. The preimage carries direct economic meaning: $|f^{-1}(σ)|/n!$ equals the probability that random serial dictatorship selects $σ$, and $f^{-1}(σ)$ is the basin of attraction of $σ$, quantifying robustness to the assignment of initial property rights. We analyze the enumeration's complexity and report experiments on preimage structure.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at PRIMA 2026 (https://www.prima2026.org/)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Thompson Sampling for Learning in Zero-Sum Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Thompson sampling (TS) achieves logarithmic and asymptotically optimal regret in classical stochastic bandits, but its behavior in multi-agent learning remains less understood. We study TS in an unknown finite two-player zero-sum matrix game with Gaussian bandit feedback. Under centralized self-play, TS samples a single payoff matrix from the posterior and plays a Nash equilibrium of the sampled game. For every fixed zero-sum game with a unique Nash equilibrium, we show that the expected cumulative duality gap is $O(\sqrt T)$. The rate improves to $O(\log T)$ for pure equilibria. We then identify the exact coefficient of the $\sqrt T$ term, which depends only on the equilibrium strategies and the noise level. We also establish a minimax lower bound matching the square-root dependence on $T$ and an instance-dependent lower bound matching the logarithmic dependence on $T$ for a class of games with a unique pure equilibrium. Experiments support the predicted rates and coefficient.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Improving the Bounds on Approximating Weighted Maximin Share for Chores
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We investigate the problem of allocating indivisible chores among agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative cost functions. An allocation is said to be $α$-weighted-maximin-share (WMMS) fair if the cost incurred by each agent is at most $α$ times her weighted maximin share. We establish that every instance admits a $4.124234528$-WMMS allocation. Moreover, for instances in which all weights and costs are rational numbers represented in binary, we give an algorithm that computes a $4.12424$-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the total binary encoding length of the input. Complementing these upper bounds, we construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs for which the optimal WMMS approximation factors converge to $e$. Together, our results substantially narrow the previously best-known gap of $[2,12]$ established by Li et al.~\cite{LWX26} to $[e,4.12424]$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Robust Proportionality Axioms for Additive Utilities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the model of participatory budgeting, in which a subset of candidates is selected subject to a budget constraint. Voters express their preferences by assigning a numerical utility to each candidate. Our focus is on formal analysis of proportionality, a central notion of fairness in multi-winner elections. Intuitively, proportionality means that each group of voters should influence the election outcome roughly in proportion to its size. Recent "plus" axioms of proportionality are particularly appealing notions: they are verifiable in polynomial time, and they provide strong representation guarantees without requiring groups of voters to have cohesive preferences. However, their existing formulations are restricted to approval-based preferences. We generalise extended justified representation plus (EJR+), and Core plus (Core+) to general additive utilities. Our approach builds on a payment-based interpretation of proportionality: candidates' costs are shared among their supporters, with the aim of balancing voters' total payments.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Lasso Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study games on finite graphs with labelled or weighted edges in which plays end as soon as the first loop is formed. The resulting play has a lasso shape: a path (head) followed by a cycle (loop). We consider two semantics for determining the winner: the loop semantics, where only the loop matters, and the lasso semantics, where the entire play is taken into account. We show that adopting the lasso semantics may have a dramatic impact on both the complexity of the game and the memory required to play optimally. Mean-payoff games with lasso semantics are no longer positionally determined, and the threshold problem â deciding whether the value of the game is at least 0 â is PSPACE-complete. In contrast, lasso parity games are equivalent to weak parity games, remain positionally determined and are solvable in polynomial time. Furthermore, we show that if a positionally determined winning objective is closed under cyclic permutation and both the objective and its complement are closed under concatenation, then it is equivalent to the parity objective. Finally, we consider mod-k games, where the winner depends on the length of the path modulo k >= 2. We show that these games, in both semantics, are PSPACE-complete. Alongside computational complexity, we analyze the memory required to play optimally. We establish that for any game positionally determined in loop semantics, memory of size 2^n is sufficient in lasso semantics. We complement this by showing exponential memory lower bounds for lasso mean-payoff and mod-k games.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: In Proceedings GandALF 2026, arXiv:2610.08898

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Representation Theorems for Actual Powers over Two-Agent General Concurrent Game Frames
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: One of the most well-known connections between logic and games is Pauly's representation theorem: the induced powers of individuals and coalitions in concurrent game frames correspond, in a precise sense, to a certain class of neighborhood frames. The precise sense here is what is called alpha effectivity (or alpha power): the power of a coalition is characterized by the sets of states in which it can ensure that the outcome lies by taking some joint action. This definition is inherently monotonic, and, as pointed out by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019), that fact can obscure relevant information about the power structure in the game: we do not know whether two sets that a coalition has the power to enforce correspond to the same joint action or to different joint actions. An alternative is to characterize the power of a coalition by its actual power (called basic power by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019)): the collection of sets of states, each of which corresponds to one joint action by the coalition and all possible joint actions by the other agents. It has recently been argued by Li and Ju (2025, 2026) that standard concurrent game frames rely on three assumptions that may, in some cases, be too strong: seriality, independence of agents, and determinism. This yields a total of eight different classes of general concurrent game frames. In this paper, assuming two agents, we prove that, in terms of actual powers, the eight classes of general concurrent game frames are represented by eight corresponding classes of neighborhood frames. This generalizes a result by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019).
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: In Proceedings GandALF 2026, arXiv:2610.08898. Corresponding author: Fengkui Ju

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Randomized Algorithm for MMS Allocation of Chores with Online Agent Arrivals
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the fair allocation of $m$ indivisible chores among $n$ agents in the agent-arrival model against an oblivious adversary. The chore set and the number of agents are known in advance. When agent $i$ arrives, her nonnegative additive cost function $c_i$ is revealed, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably assign her a subset of the unallocated chores. We focus on the notion of maximin share (MMS) and measure the fairness of the realized allocation $X$ by the ex-post MMS approximation ratio $ρ(X)$. We measure an algorithm's performance by its expected ratio, and also the guarantees that hold with high probability.
  For binary additive costs, we achieve an expected ex-post MMS ratio of $3/2+o(1)$, and show that every randomized online algorithm has an expected ratio of at least $3/2-o(1)$. For every $n$, the expected ratio is at most $1.755$. A variant of our algorithm guarantees an approximation ratio of $2$ with high probability, which is optimal. % For general additive costs, we present a weighted-rounding algorithm that achieves an expected ratio of $2+o(1)$, which also holds with high probability. The expected ratio is at most $2.594$ for every $n$. We also show that similar algorithms extend to additive goods, achieving a constant expected ex-post MMS ratio and guaranteeing every agent an $x$-fraction of her MMS with probability at least $1-85x^2$ for every $x\le1/15$.
