Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Polynomial Algorithms for Simultaneous Share-Based and Envy-Based Guarantees
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the simultaneous achievement of share-based and envy-based fairness in the allocation of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations. The AnyPrice share (APS) is a strengthening of the maximin share (MMS). A polynomial-time algorithm is known to guarantee a $2n/(3n-1)$ approximation of APS, but without an accompanying envy-based guarantee. Separately, allocations simultaneously satisfying minimum EFX share (MXS) and envy-freeness up to one less-preferred good (EFL), and subsequently the stronger requirement of residual maximin share (RMMS) together with EFL, have been shown to exist. However, the known constructions do not provide pseudopolynomial-time guarantees.
  We develop algorithms that combine these share-based and envy-based fairness requirements. First, for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we give an algorithm that computes an allocation satisfying exact EFL, $(1-\varepsilon)$-MXS, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Its running time is polynomial in the binary input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Thus, we match the previously established polynomial-time APS approximation while simultaneously guaranteeing exact EFL and an arbitrarily close approximation to MXS.
  Second, we provide a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously guarantees exact MXS, exact EFL, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Third, for every fixed number of agents, we obtain a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact RMMS and exact EFL.
  Finally, we establish that computing a numerical threshold between MXS and RMMS is weakly NP-hard, even for additive valuations. This identifies a computational barrier to extending our polynomial-time approach to exact MXS through independently computed residual-valid share thresholds.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Equilibrium Computation in Extensive-Form Games with Stochastic Action Sets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Extensive-form games (EFGs) are a standard model for sequential decision-making in games. A fundamental and typically implicit assumption in EFGs is that players always have access to all of their actions at every decision point. However, in many settings, certain actions might be unavailable during game-play due to exogenous stochasticity. Given a base EFG, we formalize a model that allows for actions to be stochastically restricted, leading to a corresponding Extensive-Form Game with Stochastic Action Sets (EFGSAS). In EFGSAS, we derive an expansion procedure that results in an equivalent EFG, thus showing that standard strategy formalisms could require exponentially large representations. However, under an appropriate independence assumption, we show that approximate compact strategy representations polynomial in the size of the base EFG exist. Computationally, we introduce an algorithm called CAT-CFR, which minimizes ranking regret and whose averaged induced sequence-form strategies converge to approximate Nash equilibria with high probability in two-player zero-sum EFGSAS. Finally, we utilize a stochastic approximation procedure to recover compact representations of approximate Nash equilibria, utilizing the iterates of CAT-CFR and additional action availability samples.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 50 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Game-Theoretic Understandings of Multi-Agent Systems with Multiple Objectives
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Agents in many multi-agent systems must balance several, possibly conflicting, objectives, and the trade-offs an agent can achieve depend on how the other agents behave. We study this setting through the Multi-Objective Markov Game (MOMG), a Markov game in which each agent receives a vector of rewards, and adopt the Pareto-Nash Equilibrium (PNE) as the solution concept: at a PNE, no agent can unilaterally improve one of its objectives without sacrificing another. We show that PNEs always exist and coincide with the Nash equilibria of the linearly scalarized games with strictly positive weights, so standard single-objective Markov-game solvers suffice to compute them. We further define the Weak Pareto-Nash Equilibrium (WPNE), which excludes only unilateral deviations that strictly improve all objectives at once. The associated gap (WPNG) is zero exactly at WPNEs and never exceeds the Nash gap of any linearly scalarized game; hence an approximate Nash equilibrium of a scalarized game is also an approximate WPNE. When the preference profile is known in advance, learning in an MOMG therefore reduces to learning in a single scalarized Markov game, for which we provide a sample-efficient algorithm. When preferences are revealed only after data collection, we design a two-phase algorithm that first explores without any preference information; with high probability, every Nash equilibrium of the learned scalarized game is then an approximate WPNE for every queried preference profile, and the WPNG of any policy can be estimated accurately from the learned model. Experiments on tabular games and four multi-objective multi-agent environments illustrate the theory and show the effect of preference-free exploration.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: EIP-4844 gave Ethereum rollups a separate fee dimension for data, governed by a multiplicative update rule that targets three ``blobs'' per block. Whether this target is reached depends on how many independent, self-interested rollups choose to post data, a question that closed-form models address only for a single agent under exogenous prices or in a static equilibrium. We propose a calibrated multi-agent reinforcement learning environment for the blob fee market in which the blob base fee is endogenous, set by the EIP-4844 rule on the aggregated decisions of heterogeneous rollups fit to post-Dencun Ethereum data. After confirming that the environment reproduces the known single-agent analytical optimum, we show that independent learners, with no convergence guarantee, still settle near the target without coordination ($3.32\pm0.01$ blobs per block over five seeds). Over a fiftyfold demand range ($10\times$ to $500\times$), supply stays at the target from $10\times$ to $200\times$ and rises above it at higher demand, where the fee can no longer hold it. Posting frequency increases with rollup size, an emergent analog of the size threshold predicted by prior theory. A costless layer-1 calldata outside option pushes the fee down by roughly an order of magnitude while aggregate supply stays at the target, so the fee rule acts as a negative-feedback controller on decentralized supply.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Internet of Things (AIBThings 2026)

Information Retrieval.title: Application based Evaluation of an Efficient Spike-Encoder, "Spiketrum"
Information Retrieval.summary: Spike-based encoders represent information as sequences of spikes or pulses, which are transmitted between neurons. A prevailing consensus suggests that spike-based approaches demonstrate exceptional capabilities in capturing the temporal dynamics of neural activity and have the potential to provide energy-efficient solutions for low-power applications. The Spiketrum encoder efficiently compresses input data using spike trains or code sets (for non-spiking applications) and is adaptable to both hardware and software implementations, with lossless signal reconstruction capability. The paper proposes and assesses Spiketrum's hardware, evaluating its output under varying spike rates and its classification performance with popular spiking and non-spiking classifiers, and also assessing the quality of information compression and hardware resource utilization. The paper extensively benchmarks both Spiketrum hardware and its software counterpart against state-of-the-art, biologically-plausible encoders. The evaluations encompass benchmarking criteria, including classification accuracy, training speed, and sparsity when using encoder outputs in pattern recognition and classification with both spiking and non-spiking classifiers. Additionally, they consider encoded output entropy and hardware resource utilization and power consumption of the hardware version of the encoders. Results demonstrate Spiketrum's superiority in most benchmarking criteria, making it a promising choice for various applications. It efficiently utilizes hardware resources with low power consumption, achieving high classification accuracy. This work also emphasizes the potential of encoders in spike-based processing to improve the efficiency and performance of neural computing systems.
Information Retrieval.comment: Under review in "IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence"

Information Retrieval.title: How Shared Representations Become Specialized: Formation, Maintenance, and Latent Susceptibility
Information Retrieval.summary: When several predictions use the same internal representation, information about some targets can remain easier to recover than information about others. We study how this specialization forms, persists, and changes in minimal artificial learners. With reconstruction errors weighted equally during learning, changing which target is observed precisely selects the favored target and redirects an already specialized learner. Removing current support can reduce a formed bias, whereas state-following update feedback can maintain it. We then compare learners formed through different observation and update conditions but matched on specified reconstruction measurements. Both change under the same brief opposing intervention, yet their responses differ. Resetting Adam largely removes the ten-update difference; exchanging its second moment reverses which route is more susceptible. New interventions show that equalizing the mean second-moment scaling reduces but does not remove the difference: its coordinate-wise pattern also matters. With fresh Adam or calibrated SGD, smaller route differences emerge later, whereas 500 common opposing updates bring the selected allocation endpoints close. A further control produces response differences with identical acquisition and equal mean loss weights but jointly different weight variability and realized sequence. Acquisition-selected formation also extends to a symmetric three-target setting. These interventions distinguish specialization's formation, present support, and time-dependent latent susceptibility.
Information Retrieval.comment: 23 pages including appendices; 5 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Learned Structure Shows Up Earlier in the Task's Own Basis: A Controlled Look at a Synchronisation Precursor in Grokking
Information Retrieval.summary: Analyses of grokking usually read hidden activations in one basis, most often the Fourier basis modulo $p$. We ask how much the answer to "has the network organised yet?" depends on that choice. The measure FSD$_{\rm gen}$ averages each unit's activation over inputs with the same answer and counts how many units share the same strongest irreducible representation. For modular multiplication we read one answer-averaged profile in three orders: discrete-logarithm order, in which the characters of the multiplicative group become Fourier modes; natural order; and random orders. Across 60 networks at $p\in\{59,97,113\}$, the discrete-log reading reached a fixed threshold before both other readings in 60 of 60 networks (59 of 60 when it had to hold 500 steps). Because untrained networks already score higher in discrete-log order, we also required an equal rise above each reading's untrained level; the discrete-log reading was still first in at least 16 of 20 networks at every prime. At $p=59$ and $p=97$ this happened during the memorisation plateau in 35 of 39 networks; at $p=113$ in 12 of 20. Memorisation preceded grokking in all 179 runs that grokked, by more than any synchronisation signal on average, so a lead over grokking is not by itself evidence of a detected circuit. Synchronisation time is only weakly related to grokking time (pooled $ρ=0.18$). On six finite groups, read with the same measure in every basis, the irreducible-representation reading came before random element orders on all six; with equal-rise thresholds this held in every case on four groups, in 7 of 10 on $\mathbb{Z}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_5$ and in none on $D_{16}$, where about half the profile power lies in one-dimensional representations the measure leaves out. We also correct a conjugate-pair artefact that roughly halves the measure on abelian groups. This version withdraws the causal and predictive claims of v1.
Information Retrieval.comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Replaces v1: the causal and predictive claims of v1 are withdrawn; see Appendix A

Information Retrieval.title: Neuromorphic Computing Based on Parametrically-Driven Oscillators and Frequency Combs
Information Retrieval.summary: Parametrically driven oscillators exhibit distinct dynamical regimes that strongly influence their computational capability as physical reservoirs. Here, we demonstrate reservoir computing in a two-mode system exhibiting 2:1 parametric resonance using Mackey--Glass, Rössler, and Lorenz chaotic time-series prediction tasks. Mapping the normalized mean squared error over parameter space reveals that the lowest prediction errors consistently occur within the parametric resonance regime, where nonlinear interactions are activated while temporal coherence is preserved. In contrast, although frequency-comb states increase spectral dimensionality, prediction performance degrades in the chaotic comb regime due to loss of phase coherence. We further show that the modulation depth $Δ\text{F}$, detuning $κ$, damping ratio $γ_{21}$, and input data rate systematically reshape the accessible dynamical regimes and thereby control the reservoir performance. These results identify parametric resonance as a robust operating regime for oscillator-based neuromorphic computing and establish dynamical regime engineering as a route toward physical reservoir optimization.
Information Retrieval.comment: 7 pages, 5 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Employing Discrete Fourier Transform in Representation Learning
Information Retrieval.summary: Image representation learning via input reconstruction is a common technique in machine learning for generating representations that can be effectively utilized by arbitrary downstream tasks. A well-established approach uses autoencoders to extract latent representations at the network's compression point. These representations are valuable because they retain essential information necessary for reconstructing the original input from the compressed latent space. In this paper, we propose an alternative learning objective. Instead of using the raw input as the reconstruction target, we employ the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of the input. The DFT provides meaningful global information at each frequency level, making individual frequency components useful as separate learning targets. When dealing with multidimensional input data, the DFT offers remarkable flexibility by enabling selective transformation across specific dimensions while preserving others in the computation. Moreover, certain types of input exhibit distinct patterns in their frequency distributions, where specific frequency components consistently contain most of the magnitude, allowing us to focus on a subset of frequencies rather than the entire spectrum. These characteristics position the DFT as a viable learning objective for representation learning. We validate our approach on the CIFAR-10 and STL-10 datasets under constrained training regimes. We discovered that integrating data augmentation during pretraining enhances the learned representations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that training exclusively on the lower-frequency components, those containing the highest magnitudes, produces results comparable to using the full frequency spectrum with only minimal reductions in accuracy.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted and published in Proceedings of ANNPR 2026 (LNCS, Springer)

Information Retrieval.title: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming
Information Retrieval.summary:
Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis.
  We catalog REPRO's behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100\% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior. Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper.
Information Retrieval.comment: Under Review for ACM TOSEM

Information Retrieval.title: CoFlu-Brain: An fMRI Connectivity Foundation Model with Cofluctuation-Based Pretraining
Information Retrieval.summary: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) commonly characterizes large-scale brain organization through functional connectivity (FC). However, an observed FC matrix is not a fixed brain graph but a statistical estimate determined by the finite BOLD frames used to compute it. Conventional FC-based approaches typically represent each scan with a single Pearson-correlation matrix, leaving frame-resolved variations in regional interactions unexploited. To address this limitation, we introduce CoFlu-Brain, which organizes framewise cofluctuation observations into multiple retained and dropped views, each summarized as an FC matrix. The model learns connectivity structure reproducible across retained views and predicts the representations of the corresponding dropped views, while adopting SIGReg from LeJEPA to prevent representation collapse. We pretrained CoFlu-Brain on 13,444 subjects from eight dataset groups and evaluated its representations via frozen-encoder linear probing on seven classification and two age-prediction tasks across seven datasets. CoFlu-Brain showed strong transfer across demographic, developmental, and clinical prediction tasks, outperforming the evaluated released models on most tasks. Random frame partitioning improved aggregate transfer, while the complete objective achieved the strongest overall performance. Code is available.

Information Retrieval.title: FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies
Information Retrieval.summary: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($τ$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.
Information Retrieval.comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at ICONIP 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Deterministic Metric Distortion of Top-2 Voting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We give tight bounds on the metric distortion of top-2 deterministic voting mechanisms. We first exploit the restrictive structure of top-2 voting to reduce the space of worst-case metrics from the continuum of biased metrics to $2^n$ subset metrics, where every candidate has distance $0$ or $1$ to the optimal candidate and $n$ is the number of candidates. We then reduce these further to just $2n$ polar metrics: $n$ of these have a single optimal candidate, and the other $n$ have a single sub-optimal candidate. This reduction yields an efficient algorithm that computes the exact distortion of every candidate on a given profile and runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time. As a corollary, we can derive the exact worst-case distortion for top-2 voting for all values of $n$, for which previous work had non-matching lower and upper bounds.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 9 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two-dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co-player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co-player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long-term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always-defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit-for-tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 27 pages, 14 figures (12 pages + 3 figures main text; 15 pages + 11 figures Supplemental Material). Code: https://github.com/james-wolfe/reactive-learning

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Can You Trust Your Preference Models? Stackelberg Games for Alignment
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. We formulate this search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between two opposing policies, a Leader which tries to minimize disagreement, and a Follower which maximizes it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games, we establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness and a closed-form characterization. We introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (SMIDA), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting, and develop a neural policy-gradient analogue. Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error. On held out data the trained policies outperform reference policies and increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Division via Subsidies
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the relationship between fair division with $\textit{subsidies}$ and $\textit{best-of-both-worlds}$ (BoBW) fairness for indivisible items. We prove a general reduction of BoBW existence to envy-freeability. Specifically, for any scale-free ex-post property $P$ (e.g., EF1, EFX, PO) and any scale-free valuation class $\mathcal{V}$ (e.g, additive, submodular, subadditive, monotone), if every instance in $\mathcal{V}$ admits a $P$-allocation that can be made envy-free using subsidies, then every such instance admits an ex-ante envy-free lottery supported on $P$-allocations. The proof uses linear programming duality. As applications, the reduction gives alternative proofs of BoBW existence results for additive goods, chores, and mixtures of goods and chores. The converse of our general reduction holds for two agents but fails for three: We provide a four-good counterexample with monotone submodular valuations where an ex-ante envy-free and ex-post EF1 lottery exists, but no allocation is simultaneously EF1 and envy-freeable. For lexicographic valuations, we prove simultaneous EFX, Pareto optimality, and envy-freeability (and hence BoBW guarantees for EFX+PO) for three agents, and show that even EFX and envy-freeability can be incompatible for four agents.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 16 pages in main body, 1 page appendix

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: MILP the Gap: An Automated Reasoning Approach to Condorcet's Paradox
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Computational social choice studies how conflicting individual preferences are aggregated into a collective decision, with applications to elections, AI evaluation/alignment, and recommendation systems. We focus on settings where $n$ voters (e.g., human evaluators or algorithmic benchmarks) each rank $m$ alternatives (e.g., human candidates or AI models/outputs), and the goal is to select a committee of $k$ alternatives. One measure of the (in)stability of the outcome is the number of voters who prefer an unchosen alternative to all alternatives in the committee. If this number is less than half the electorate, the committee is a Condorcet winning set, which may not exist if $k \leq 2$. More generally, there exist instances where any committee of size $k$ has at least a $\frac{2}{(k+1)}-ε$ fraction of the electorate preferring another alternative, for arbitrarily small $ε$. While recent work has made remarkable progress narrowing the gap, it is currently unknown whether this lower bound is tight. We develop a mixed-integer linear programming framework that computes exact bounds for fixed parameter values. Our approach depends only on $m$ and $k$; by modeling electorates as distributions over rankings, we eliminate any dependence on $n$. Our programs allow us to rule out counterexamples over arbitrary electorate sizes and obtain tight bounds for fixed $m$ and $k$. Further, our framework provides a pathway for proving general upper bounds. In particular, we show a linear regime, $k \ge \frac{8m}{9}$, in which the conjectured $\frac{2}{(k+1)}$ upper bound indeed holds, providing the first results that match known lower bounds. Beyond stability, our framework can characterize the relationships among other social choice axioms, which we demonstrate by producing minimal incomparability results.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: An earlier version titled "Is Four Enough? Automated Reasoning Approaches and Dual Bounds for Condorcet Dimensions of Elections" appears at the 8th Games, Agents, and Incentives Workshop (GAIW-26), held as part of the Workshops at the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Beyond Independent Values: Optimal Auctions with Correlated Valuations for LLM-Native Advertising
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Conversational assistants are becoming the place where people ask what to buy, and sponsored content is moving into their answers. Several advertisers then compete for one sponsored slot, and all of them read the same conversation, so their willingness to pay usually moves together. Existing auctions for LLM advertising treat these values as independent. We therefore present AffMyerson, an auction that captures this correlation and turns it into revenue. We model the advertisers' values given the conversation as a multivariate normal and turn the economic premise of positive dependence (affiliation) into a sign condition on the precision matrix. We design a neural parameterization whose every output satisfies it. We prove that every prior in this family yields a truthful, ex-post individually rational auction, so estimation error can cost revenue but never truthfulness. We derive the conditional virtual values in closed form. By the design of the prior, pricing an auction needs no matrix inversion and takes O(n^2) time, fast enough to run at query time. We also work out the log-normal family used in empirical ad-auction work. There we prove that the auction is truthful for every prior and revenue-optimal when the prior is correct, and that the virtual value is regular everywhere whenever the conditional spread is below a loose threshold, which our fitted priors stay well under. With LLM-agent bidders, AffMyerson earns 6.2% more than a second-price auction with a tuned reserve, 6.1% more than Ronen's lookahead auction with the same prior, and 9.2% more than Myerson's auction run as if values were independent. This gain is still 4.5% on real keyword search queries where willingness to pay is hard to read. The correlation comes from common demand. Agents that judge the conversation bid together and agents told to calculate do not. The gain from conditioning moves with the correlation.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 23 pages, 4 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We propose a new framework for banner ad auctions, leveraging diffusion models to allow for multiple bidders to co-win a single banner ad opportunity, and in particular influence the ad shown on the banner depending on the strength of their bids, enabling a far richer outcome space compared to standard banner ad auctions, where there is a single winner who shows their ad. In our framework, the outcomes are images (what ad to show) and each bidder expresses their preferences over outcomes by declaring their value per unit of alignment between the image chosen by the mechanism and a textual description of their desired image. Our proposed mechanism combines the advertisers' bids and textual descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model. This is used to sample a set of candidate images from which the welfare maximizing one is eventually chosen. Extensive experimentation evaluates our proposed mechanism around the following axes: (1) efficiency improvements of our allocation rule relative to the single-winner allocation rule; (2) monotonicity of our allocation rule; and (3) approximate incentive compatibility when combining our allocation rule with Myerson lemma-based or Clarke rule-based payments. Improvements along all these axes are shown with the number of Monte Carlo samples. Meanwhile, these benefits are attained while preserving the image quality.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Appeared in EC 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Beyond a Single Optimal Design: A Dynamical Systems Characterization of Online Allocation with Convex Costs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study online allocation with convex costs (\OACC), a generalization of limited-supply models in which additional resources can be produced dynamically at convex cost. Prior work largely focuses on constructing a single algorithm that achieves strong competitive guarantees. In contrast, our main contribution is a structural characterization of the optimal design space of reserve functions (i.e., normalized pricing rules) for \OACC, yielding a family of optimal online algorithms.
  Using a principled dynamical-systems approach, we show that optimal online algorithms arise as solutions of a nonlinear eigenvalue problem: the optimal competitive ratio corresponds to the dominant eigenvalue, and the associated eigenfunction determines the optimal reserve function. This perspective establishes the existence of infinitely many optimal designs attaining the best possible competitive ratio, thereby unifying and generalizing a broad class of prior algorithms. Beyond unification, our characterization uncovers new structural phenomena, including the ability to flexibly mix dynamic and static pricing without loss of optimality and the construction of universally competitive algorithms under unknown or stochastic costs. We further extend the analysis to more structured settings such as supply-oblivious arrivals and hard supply constraints, obtaining sharper guarantees that improve upon previous bounds.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at WINE 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Randomly Wrong Signals: Bayesian Auction Design with ML Predictions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Machine learning can help sellers predict buyers' willingness to pay, but its predictions may be plausible and yet entirely unrelated to a buyer's value. We introduce a Bayesian auction model that distinguishes such hallucinations from ordinary measurement noise. We characterize revenue-maximizing auctions with publicly disclosed predictions in the benchmark where informative predictions are exact. For a single buyer, this characterization explains when the seller should follow a prediction and when to hedge against its failure by ignoring it or capping the price. These insights guide the design of simple auctions that account for both hallucinations and measurement noise. Numerical experiments show that the resulting auctions achieve near-optimal revenue.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Revenue Maximization in Choice-Based Matching Markets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The primary contribution of this paper resides in devising constant-factor approximation guarantees for revenue maximization in two-sided matching markets with general pairwise rewards. A major distinction between our work and state-of-the-art results in this context (Ashlagi et al., 2022; Torrico et al., 2023) is that, for the first time, we are able to address reward maximization, reflected by assigning each customer-supplier pair an arbitrarily-valued reward. Our performance guarantees apply to two different settings: the customized model and the inclusive model. The fundamental difference between these settings lies in whether the platform should display to each supplier all selecting customers, as in the inclusive model, or whether the platform can further personalize this set, as in the customized model. Technically speaking, our algorithmic approaches and their analysis revolve around presenting a closely related combinatorial problem, a novel linear relaxation, and developing tailor-made analytical ideas. In both models considered, these ingredients allow us to overcome the lack of submodularity and subadditivity that stems from pairwise rewards, plaguing the applicability of existing methods. We complement our theoretical results with an extensive computational study under different classes of instances where we analyze the empirical reward and running time performance of our proposed methods.

Information Retrieval.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
Information Retrieval.summary: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted to AXIOM: Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning (NeurIPS 2026 workshop). 4 pages + appendix, 4 figures, 5 tables

Information Retrieval.title: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
Information Retrieval.summary: Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. An output head maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, from which an autoregressive decoder constructs a feasible solution. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 MLxOR workshop. Paper contains 6 pages (4 main text, 1 references, 1 appendix); 1 figure and 3 tables

Information Retrieval.title: When LLMs Develop Languages: Symbolic Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning
Information Retrieval.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves large language models (LLMs) on difficult reasoning tasks, but it often incurs long natural-language rationales that are poorly aligned with efficient machine reasoning. We propose Communicative Language Symbolism Routing (CLSR), a test-time framework in which multiple LLM agents autonomously invent, evolve, and share compact Language Symbolism Frameworks (LSFs), while a latent-free router adaptively selects and composes these languages per query to optimize the accuracy-token trade-off. Unlike prompt optimization that refines surface instructions, CLSR treats each LSF as a reusable symbolic protocol with compact symbols, usage rules, and a message-passing contract, and improves it through an evolutionary loop driven by correctness and token cost. At inference time, the router may invoke a single low-cost LSF call, ensemble multiple LSFs, or execute a multi-round LSF composition protocol on harder queries. Across challenging benchmarks, CLSR reduces latency-oriented generated token completion by $3\sim 6\times$ compared to standard CoT while maintaining accuracy. We further derive an information-theoretic lower bound on token cost under arbitrary symbolism and show that, under an interpreter-realizability premise, multi-round LSF protocols conditionally subsume program-execution pipelines. Code is publicly available (https://github.com/pzqpzq/LSF_MDia).
Information Retrieval.comment: ICML2026 Regular paper

Information Retrieval.title: Large Language Model-Guided Evolutionary Discovery of Native Neural Architectures for Spiking Sequence Modeling
Information Retrieval.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer low-energy sequence modeling through sparse, event-driven computation. However, interactions among spike encoding, neuronal dynamics, and information propagation complicate architecture design. Existing SNN sequence models often adapt artificial neural network (ANN) architectures designed for real-valued activations, potentially underusing spike-based communication and temporal state updates, motivating automated discovery of native SNN architectures. Most evolutionary neural architecture search (ENAS) methods operate within predefined configuration spaces, limiting discovery to mechanisms expressible within those spaces. We introduce OpenArchEvo, which uses large language models (LLMs) to evolve executable architecture code in an open program space under spiking-projection constraints. In this space, code differences need not reflect architectural novelty, while direct performance evaluation requires costly training. We construct a three-view representation spanning code, design rationale, and a behavioral fingerprint to support novelty estimation and performance prediction. The search treats predicted performance and estimated novelty as two objectives, using surrogate predictions to select candidates for expensive training evaluations. With an estimated candidate-training cost of 132 V100 GPU-days, the search uncovers multiple native SNN architectures, exemplified by three designs featuring mechanisms such as spike-activity-dependent control of state updates and residual pathways. The discovered NeuroGate surpasses the ANN DeltaNet on WikiText-103, and the discovered architectures reduce estimated architecture-level arithmetic energy by up to 50.6x (LoopMem) relative to a common dense Transformer (ANN) baseline. Code and all discovered architectures: https://github.com/Optima-CityU/OpenArchEvo
Information Retrieval.comment: 38 pages (15 pages main text + appendix), 12 figures, 10 tables. Code: https://github.com/Optima-CityU/OpenArchEvo

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration with an ERM Oracle
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: A predictor is multicalibrated with respect to a class of subpopulations (formally, of functions on the inputs, called auditors) if, for every subpopulation in the class and every value the predictor outputs, the average outcome among the members of that subpopulation who receive that value is close to the value itself. For finite classes, about $\varepsilon^{-3}$ samples are necessary and sufficient to learn a predictor with multicalibration error $\varepsilon$, but the algorithms that attain this rate enumerate the class, which is impossible for the large classes of interest. We ask how many samples suffice when the learner accesses the class only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples and polynomially many ERM calls, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the class. Its dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal for all learners. When $d$ is at least about $1/\varepsilon$, every learner that can only access the class through polynomially many ERM calls needs $\tildeΩ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples. Learners with unlimited computation need only $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}+d\varepsilon^{-2})$ samples, so the extra factor $1/\varepsilon$ on the dimension term is the price of oracle efficiency. For swap multicalibration, which allows a different function from the class for each predicted value, $\tildeΘ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples are necessary and sufficient. For estimating the error of a given predictor, the ordinary notion is the harder one: the swap error can be estimated with an ERM oracle, whereas the ordinary error is NP-hard to approximate even for classes with linear-time ERM. Consequently, there are classes for which it is computationally easier to learn a multicalibrated predictor than to compute the multicalibration error of a given predictor.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 58 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Assortment Optimization under the Mallows Model: Independent-Utility Choice Equivalence and Its Algorithmic Implications
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The Mallows model is a well-established construct in preference modeling, describing random rankings through their Kendall-Tau distance from a reference permutation. Its compact parameterization and interpretable treatment of preference uncertainty have made it influential across statistics, machine learning, probability, and revenue management. In the latter domain, recent literature has studied the embedding of Mallows-driven choice into assortment optimization. Early approximation schemes in this context require stylized structural simplifications or restrictive parametric assumptions. In the absence of these levers, a highly involved quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme has subsequently been proposed, leaving wide open the question of whether near-optimal assortments can be computed in true polynomial time.
  The main contribution of this focused technical paper resides in closing these gaps by uncovering a striking independent-utility structure within Mallows choices, and turning this representation into a polynomial-time approximation scheme. Our central structural characterization explicitly constructs a single collection of mutually independent utilities, reproducing Mallows choice probabilities simultaneously for all offered sets. This exact choice equivalence connects pending Mallows-related challenges to the recent approximation framework of Bowers et al. (FOCS 2025) for assortment optimization under independent random utilities. We make this connection algorithmically feasible through a finite-support reduction that produces distributions of polynomial size while controlling revenue loss uniformly over all assortments. Fused together, these ingredients lead to an $O(n^{\tilde{O}(1/ε^2)})$-time approximation scheme for assortment optimization under the Mallows model, while allowing arbitrary product prices, concentration parameters, and modal rankings.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent Ascent is Suboptimal for Nonconvex-PŁ Min-Max Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: How far can stochastic gradient descent ascent (SGDA) go by tuning its timescale ratio and step sizes in nonconvex min-max games? We answer this question for nonconvex-PŁ (NC-PŁ) games by establishing the first tight complexity of two-timescale SGDA with a fixed timescale ratio and non-increasing step sizes. For $\ell$-smooth games with an inner $μ$-PŁ inequality, we prove a complexity lower bound $Ω(κ^2\ell\varepsilon^{-2}+κ^4\ellσ^2\varepsilon^{-4})$, where $κ=\ell/μ$ is the condition number, $σ^2$ is the gradient variance, and $\varepsilon$ measures the outer gradient norm. This matches existing SGDA upper bounds and establishes a complexity separation from Smoothed-AGDA (Yang et al., 22'). In addition, we show that SGDA can fail to find a stationary point when its timescale ratio is as small as $o(κ^2)$. Our negative results highlight the fundamental limitation of SGDA in NC-PŁ games, and justify the development of alternative methods.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Efficient Algorithms for Online Subadditive Combinatorial Allocations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: For the online combinatorial allocation problem with subadditive valuations, Correa and Cristi (STOC 2023) proved the existence of a $6$-competitive online algorithm, improving on the previous best $O(\log\!\log m)$-competitive online algorithm due to Dütting, Kesselheim, and Lucier (FOCS 2020), where $m$ is the number of items. However, Correa and Cristi's result is existential, and it was left open whether a constant competitive ratio is attainable via an efficient online algorithm that uses a polynomial number of demand oracle queries. In this work, we answer this affirmatively, giving an expected-polynomial-time $(6 + ε)$-competitive online algorithm for any constant $ε> 0$. Our techniques also recover, in the offline setting, the $(2 + ε)$-approximation result of Feige (STOC, 2006). Finally, when the buyers' valuations are drawn from identical distributions, we exploit symmetry to obtain an improved $(60/11+ε)$-competitive algorithm. Starting with the natural configuration LP relaxation for the problem, our main technical contribution is a recursive Bundle Score Generator (BSG) that resolves item conflicts by assigning correlated scores to the items requested by each buyer. Unlike the Random Score Generator whose existence is shown by Correa and Cristi, our BSG is efficiently computable in expected polynomial time. Moreover, it satisfies a stochastic dominance property that is sufficient to recover both Feige's offline result and Correa and Cristi's online result.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Smart Lotteries in School Choice: Ex-ante Pareto-Improvement with Ex-post Stability
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In school choice, students typically have strict preferences over the schools while the schools have coarse priorities over the students based on their distance and their enrolled siblings. The outcome of a centralized admission mechanism is then usually obtained by the Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm with random tie-breaking. Therefore, every outcome of this mechanism that occurs with a positive probability is a stable solution for the coarse priorities. This implies a probabilistic assignment, specifying the admission probability for each student-school pair. In this paper, we propose a new efficiency-improving stable 'smart lottery' mechanism. We aim to improve the probabilistic assignment ex-ante in a stochastic dominance sense, while ensuring that the improved random matching is still ex-post stable, meaning that it can be decomposed into stable matchings regarding the original coarse priorities. Therefore, this smart lottery mechanism can provide a clear Pareto-improvement in expectation for any cardinal utilities compared to the standard DA with lottery solution, without sacrificing the stability of the final outcome. We show that although the underlying computational problem is NP-hard, we can solve the problem in practice by using column generation. Our computational results show that the welfare gains by our mechanism are substantially larger than the expected gains by standard methods that realize efficiency improvements after ties have already been broken. Additionally, we illustrate for real-world school choice data of Ghent (Belgium) that, while not theoretically guaranteed, our mechanism can Pareto-improve upon methods that improve upon DA but violate ex-post stability, such as Efficiency-Adjusted Deferred Acceptance.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Asymmetric Information in Dynamic Lending Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study a dynamic lending game with limited but reusable supply. Borrower arrivals and loan durations are stochastic. Demand is allocated cheapest-first, subject to available supply, so a lender's quote affects both its current payoff and its ability to serve future borrowers. Motivated by industry practice, we study this problem through the lens of information disclosure: Lenders observe either only their own available supply or also their rivals' aggregate available supply. We ask how providing this information to all, some or none of the lenders affects payoffs as demand varies relative to supply, and how these effects change when a fixed total supply is divided among different numbers of lenders. Interestingly, in the case of asymmetric information disclosure, total payoffs can increase, while total lending remains the same. We identify sufficient mathematical regimes in which this phenomenon occurs. Who receives supply information matters differently as demand rises. For the case of two lenders, informing only the larger lender yields higher total lender payoff at lower demand, while informing only the smaller lender can yield the highest total lender payoff at higher demand. For a platform deciding which lenders can observe rival supply, the results suggest that disclosure can change the fees paid by borrowers without changing how much is lent. Wider access to supply information need not lower those fees: its effect depends on who receives the information and the balance between demand and supply.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 29 pages including references and appendices

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Algorithms with Smoothed Polynomial-Time Complexity for Deterministic Discounted-sum and Mean-payoff Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Turn-based deterministic games on graphs are two-player zero-sum games played on finite directed graphs, where the vertex set is partitioned between the Max and the adversarial Min Player. The respective player chooses outgoing edges from their vertices. We consider these games with the classical discounted-sum and mean-payoff objectives. The goal of the Max Player is to maximize the objective against the adversarial Min Player. These games lie in NP $\cap$ coNP and are among the rare combinatorial problems that belong to this complexity class, yet the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm is a major open question. All known deterministic algorithms require exponential time in the worst case, while the classical strategy iteration (policy iteration) algorithm is remarkably efficient in practice, which motivates the study of the smoothed complexity of these games. Previous results established a smoothed polynomial-time bound only for the restricted class of ergodic games and presented only a high-probability guarantee. Our main result is a new analysis technique for a variant of the strategy iteration algorithm, and we show these algorithms achieve smoothed polynomial complexity for general game graphs with both high-probability and expected runtime guarantees. In particular, our result removes the ergodicity restriction of prior work and strengthens the high-probability guarantee to the stronger expected-runtime guarantee, thereby resolving the open question on the smoothed complexity of these games.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Distortion of Threshold Approval Multiwinner Voting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study multiwinner voting with $n$ voters and $m$ candidates, where the goal is to select a committee of size $k$. Voters have unit-sum cardinal utilities but report only coarse information induced by $t$ utility thresholds. In particular, each voter partitions the candidates into approval sets, with the utilities of all candidates in the same set lying between the same pair of consecutive thresholds. We model the utility of each voter for a committee as a normalized monotone symmetric norm, capturing, among others, additive welfare, best-representative utility, top-$r$ welfare, $\ell_p$ welfare, and normalized non-increasing ordered weighted averages. We design a deterministic rule with distortion at most $2(2m)^{1/t}$ and a randomized rule with distortion at most $2\min\{m^{1/(t+1)},m/k\}$. These guarantees hold for every committee size $k$ and every norm in our framework. Consequently, a single threshold yields distortion $O(m)$ for deterministic rules and $O(\sqrt{m})$ for randomized rules, while $O(\log m)$ thresholds suffice for constant distortion. We complement these results with norm-dependent lower bounds that asymptotically match our upper bounds for constant committee sizes, including the single-winner case.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Complexity of Autobidding Equilibria in GSP Sponsored Shopping
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We revisit autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions, recently proposed and studied in Dütting et al. On the existence side, we show that autobidding equilibria under both budget constraints (ABE-B) and return-on-investment constraints (ABE-R) always exist and, moreover, always admit equilibria with polynomial-size support over the allocation space. On the computational side, we show that computing an exact equilibrium is in FIXP, and that computing an approximate equilibrium is in PPAD. We also prove that computing an approximate equilibrium is PPAD-hard for both ABE-B and ABE-R. Together, these results provide a fairly comprehensive picture of the computational complexity of autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Limit-sure Winning in Team Games without Shared Randomness
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study concurrent stochastic games in which a team of agents plays against an adversarial environment. If the agents could access a shared source of randomness, then these games reduce to two-player games. Despite being common in the literature on coalition games, this assumption does not accurately model real-world systems. In this paper, we consider the setting where the agents only have access to individual sources of randomness, and must satisfy a given reachability or safety objective. The limit-sure problem asks whether the team can ensure that the objective is satisfied with probability at least $1-λ$ for every $λ>0$. For reachability objectives, we show that this problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete. For safety objectives, we show that limit-sure winning coincides with almost-sure winning, which is known to lie in $\mathsf{P}$. As a corollary of these results, we conclude that model checking of the qualitative fragment of the logic Individually Randomised ATL -- introduced in the recent work of Brice et al. -- is $\mathsf{P}^{\mathsf{NP}}$-complete.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 31 pages, 6 figures. Full version with appendix

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Protocol effects on feature-based hardware-Trojan detection across Trust-Hub families
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Trust-Hub reuses host circuits: several files differ mainly in the inserted Trojan. When gates from sibling variants enter both training and test folds, a detector can benefit from host logic it has already seen. We measure that effect instead of proposing another classifier. The corpus contains 49,124 gates from 16 netlists grouped into five host families. We left the parser, 36 gate features, class weighting, model settings, threshold, and family-level aggregation unchanged and altered one choice: the test boundary. The three settings draw test gates from the pooled corpus, withhold a complete netlist, or withhold every variant of one host. The choice matters. Random forest records F1/AP of 0.914/0.978 with pooled gates, 0.636/0.851 with one netlist held out, and 0.460/0.577 with a host family held out. XGBoost falls from 0.946/0.976 to 0.464/0.544 across the same comparison. Logistic regression loses AP, although its fixed-threshold F1 is not monotonic. Each family shows the same pooled-to-family direction. Feature removal, repeated model and simulator seeds, score normalization, parser-related exclusions, and a smaller sample change the size of the gap without reversing it. Aggregation also matters: a gate-weighted average is dominated by the larger ISCAS files, so the headline values give each host family one vote. Bootstrap and jackknife summaries keep the gap positive, but their folds reuse training families. We treat the five family rows as descriptive evidence rather than independent trials. Five host families are too few for a population claim, and the experiment says nothing about transfer to a new cell library or an industrial design. It supports a narrower conclusion: sibling benchmark variants can inflate apparent transfer. Benchmarks with several variants of one host circuit should report family-aware holdouts and all five family results beside pooled scores.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 table. Accepted at IEEE ICCSIE 2026. Author accepted manuscript. Reproducibility artifact: https://zenodo.org/records/23230179

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases. We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020]
  Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents). These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Co-opetition Equilibrium in Adversarial Team Games with Heterogeneous Utilities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The United Nations' 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development requires all countries to collaborate against adversarial factors, a scenario that can be formalized as an adversarial team game. However, existing solution concepts assume team players share identical utility functions---an assumption inconsistent with real-world settings where countries have divergent objectives. This paper argues that studying adversarial team games must account for heterogeneous utilities among team players. We show that ignoring utility differences can render computed equilibria unstable in the original game, and we formalize this degradation via the Price of Ignoring Heterogeneity, which can be unbounded. To address this, we introduce the Co-opetition Equilibrium (CoE), where team players with heterogeneous utilities correlate their strategies (cooperation) against an adversary (competition). We establish existence via reduction from Nash equilibrium, and prove that finding a CoE is PPAD-complete while computing a Team-Maximizing CoE (TMCoE) is NP-hard. Nevertheless, we identify a broad class of zero-sum adversarial team games---those satisfying a consistent-constraint condition that generalizes identical utilities---where TMCoEs are exchangeable and computable in polynomial time via linear programming. We outline directions for algorithm design, MARL, and extensions to extensive-form and multi-team games.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: This paper was accepted by DAI 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Network Topology Shapes AI Intervention Effectiveness on Deception: Truth-Telling vs. Investigative Agents
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Deploying AI agents to combat dishonest communication is an intuitive response to deception in hybrid human-AI societies. However, the efficacy of such interventions in realistic networked settings remains unclear. We study this problem using an evolutionary game-theoretic model of the Deceiver's Game by extending it to structured networks, where agents can adopt deception, truth-telling, and investigation strategies. We introduce committed AI agents (zealots) fixed to either truth-telling or investigative strategies and conduct agent-based simulations across three network topologies. Our key findings are: (1) passive committed truth-telling agents can amplify adaptive deception by creating exploitable honest partners, whereas investigative agents increase adaptive truth-telling in the oscillatory regime; (2) intervention effects are non-monotonic in deployment density because committed agents reshape rather than simply suppress the underlying oscillatory dynamics; and (3) response peaks depend on topology, with sampled scale-free populations showing sharp low-density responses and fully connected populations requiring larger committed fractions. Overall, the results highlight the need to distinguish passive truth-telling from active investigation when using committed agents to influence networked deception dynamics.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.

Information Retrieval.title: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? Two Reasons for Shrinking Importance Estimates in Continual Learning
Information Retrieval.summary: Regularization-based continual learning protects each parameter in proportion to an estimate of its importance, yet these estimates come from finite samples and heuristics and are used as if they were exact. We report four studies that start from a biologically inspired mechanism and end with a statistical explanation of it. Motivated by dendritic nanotubes, we let transient lateral links diffuse importance tags between hidden units. Links between co-active units gave no significant gain, but random links with lifetimes of 25 or 200 steps raised final accuracy on 20-task Permuted MNIST by 1.5 to 2.6 points. We show that random diffusion implements linear shrinkage of importance toward the layer mean in expectation. A simulation of the link process alone predicts shrinkage weights of 0.23 and 0.52 for these lifetimes, and graph-free shrinkage at 0.25 and 0.5 reproduces both the accuracy and the dispersion of the consolidated importance, while every activity-dependent rule did worse than random links. A five-seed screen across EWC, SI, and MAS found nominal gains for SI and MAS on Permuted MNIST and losses on task-incremental Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was small and shrinkage cost plasticity. Varying the number of importance samples then separates two mechanisms on Permuted MNIST. For EWC, the gain fell by about ten points per tenfold increase in samples, from 19.6 points with 10 samples to -0.4 with 1000, a variance effect. For MAS, a gain of about one point persisted at 1000 samples, consistent with a bias in the importance measure rather than noise. Shrinkage had no detectable effect for MAS on a domain-incremental CIFAR-100 benchmark. Finally, we show that a standard heteroscedastic empirical Bayes rule shrinks the largest Fisher-type estimates most, which may explain its poor results, and point to a log-scale alternative.
Information Retrieval.comment: Github: https://github.com/Saurav-K-Aryal/Do-Artificial-Neural-Networks-Need-Dendritic-Nanotubes-.git 21 pages, 3 figures, 10 tables. Simulation and figure scripts are included as ancillary files

Information Retrieval.title: The Value of Spike Timing: A Leakage-Resistant Benchmark of SNN Design Choices for Network Intrusion Detection
Information Retrieval.summary:
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are increasingly studied for network intrusion detection, but comparative evidence on how neuron models and spike encodings affect performance remains limited. Evaluation choices can further influence the observed results when preprocessing, capture structure, or scenario information crosses the train-test boundary. We evaluate nine snnTorch neuron families with three spike encodings, yielding 27 SNN configurations across four intrusion-detection benchmarks. We first screen the complete design space and then repeat the evaluation using train-only transforms, seed-independent partitions, and capture- or scenario-aware separation. At the shared operating point, LeakyParallel/latency achieved the lowest mean rank in both sweeps but was not statistically separated from Leaky/latency; their screening order reversed when CTU-13 was excluded. Overall, screening and confirmation retained substantial rank agreement despite changes in measured performance.
  We then examine what latency coding contributes by holding the active spike set fixed and changing only its temporal organization. At the main T=25 operating point, mapping feature magnitude to spike time improved macro-F1 on all five confirmation protocols, while spreading the same spikes through time without that mapping could either improve or reduce performance. Latency coding thus combines informative spike timing with temporal network dynamics. Sparse input encoding does not directly imply sparse internal activity, although latency coding requires fewer fanout-weighted operations than rate coding in the evaluated models. These findings motivate separate assessment of SNN design, evaluation protocol, spike timing, and computational activity for static network-flow data.

Information Retrieval.title: Evolving Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures for Image Classification
Information Retrieval.summary: Hybrid quantum classical neural networks integrate parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) with established deep learning architectures, but their performance depends strongly on the choice of quantum circuit architecture, a choice that remains largely manual. Most existing approaches rely on hand-designed or fixed circuit ansätze, requiring circuit structure, gate composition, and qubit connectivity to be specified in advance with no guarantee that they suit the task. This limitation is especially acute in image classification, where quantum circuits must transform features extracted by classical networks while remaining compact enough for practical training, requirements that generic, task-agnostic ansätze are unlikely to satisfy simultaneously. We extend EXAQC, an evolutionary framework for automated quantum circuit discovery, to image classification. EXAQC evolves PQCs as intermediate processing modules while retaining classical feature-extraction and prediction layers. On MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, EXAQC achieves 98.42%, 90.62%, and 85.47% accuracy, respectively, while using comparable gate counts to other quantum architecture-search methods. Against classical networks, evolved hybrid models maintain comparable accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters, reaching 85.68% on CIFAR-10 with over 25$\times$ fewer parameters than a 10-layer CNN. Encoding choice also matters: rotation-based encodings (RX, RY, U3) outperform amplitude encoding by 22-25 points on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that automated circuit discovery yields compact quantum modules that can replace larger classical components in vision architectures while retaining competitive accuracy.
Information Retrieval.comment: Under Review at The Fifteenth International Conference on Learning Representations 2027

Information Retrieval.title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness
Information Retrieval.summary: Clinical sleep medicine repeatedly documents profound divergences between objective sleep duration and subjective daytime impairment, notably exemplified by sleep state misperception in paradoxical insomnia and boundary instability in narcolepsy type 1. Here, we present DyssomniaNN: a multi-scale biophysical computational framework coupling Borbély's two-process regulation of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with Saper's hypothalamic reciprocal flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network. We formalize five clinical cohorts across an identical 72-hour photoperiod: healthy control, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (delayed-phase), chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. The synthetic local field potential converges closely with empirical human electroencephalography spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical frequency bands (spectral mean absolute error of 0.33--0.35). Furthermore, we introduce the Well-Rested Index to quantify restorative efficacy. Simulations reveal that sleep duration fails to predict restorative recovery: paradoxical insomnia achieves normal total sleep time (21.15 h) yet yields low restoration (37.6%) from unsuppressed cortical beta-band intrusion, whereas hypocretin deficiency in narcolepsy produces severe nocturnal fragmentation (781 min of wake after sleep onset) and 35 sleep-onset rapid eye movement periods. DyssomniaNN provides an in silico platform for mechanistic sleep research and virtual neuropharmacology.
Information Retrieval.comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables

Information Retrieval.title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
Information Retrieval.summary: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks---spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equations---the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.

Information Retrieval.title: REMBGO for Evaluation-Limited Optimization: CEC2022 Benchmarking and EAF-STATCOM Generalization
Information Retrieval.summary: Metaheuristic comparisons are often reported at evaluation budgets far larger than an expensive engineering simulation can afford. This paper presents REMBGO, an evaluation-budget-aware refinement of EMBGO. Its contribution is not any single operator: it is the integration of population preservation, scale-normalized exploration and recovery mechanisms whose parent-relative benefit is concentrated under restricted function-evaluation budgets. REMBGO is evaluated on CEC2022 at a primary, application-aligned budget of 1040 function evaluations, with a surrounding budget ladder reported descriptively to characterise budget dependence rather than as a family of controlled hypotheses. A component-removal study finds no individual mechanism whose removal survives multiplicity correction, consistent with an integrated rather than a single-operator contribution.
